item.title: Team PCP CI/CD secret theft, CVE-2026-59310 vCenter exploitation, and Chromium tradecraft
item.content:encoded:
Window: 13 Aug 14:00 → 13 Aug 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

Critical VMware vCenter RCE flaw exploited for reverse SSH access — Must Read

Attackers are actively exploiting the critical VMware vCenter Syslog Server flaw CVE-2026-59310 to install reverse_ssh for persistent remote access, with 361 victim IPs observed across 47 countries. Admins should apply Broadcom’s emergency vCenter updates immediately, as no workaround is available.

  • A recently patched critical vulnerability, CVE-2026-59310, in VMware vCenter Syslog Server is being exploited to deploy a reverse SSH tool for persistence and remote access.
  • QUIRSO identified compromises at 361 IP addresses across 47 countries, with more than half located in Germany, the U.S., Turkey, Iran, and France.
  • Broadcom disclosed CVE-2026-59310 on July 29 as a critical directory traversal vulnerability that unauthenticated attackers with network access could exploit to execute arbitrary code.
  • Broadcom provides no workarounds or mitigations and urges administrators to apply the emergency vCenter updates that fix the issue.
  • QUIRSO said compromised systems began connecting to attacker-controlled infrastructure on August 3, five days after Broadcom disclosed the flaw and released the emergency patch.

Technologies: hypervisor, remote-access

Products: vmware-vcenter, vcenter-syslog-server, reverse-ssh

Vendors: broadcom, vmware, quirso

Team PCP Stole 78,330 Secrets From 2,186 Organizations. CloudSEK Just Published the List. — Must Read

CloudSEK published a dataset showing Team PCP exfiltrated 78,330 secrets from CI/CD pipelines at 2,186 organizations in five days by compromising trusted open source components. The main takeaway is that CI/CD runners have become a major supply chain target and need production-grade controls like dependency pinning, runtime monitoring, and outbound network restrictions.

  • CloudSEK published a searchable dataset showing that Team PCP exfiltrated 78,330 distinct secrets from the CI/CD pipelines of 2,186 organizations between March 19 and March 24, 2026.
  • The exposed organizations included 92 public companies with a combined market capitalization of $6.2 trillion, according to StepSecurity’s analysis of the CloudSEK dataset.
  • StepSecurity’s analysis found that GitLab was the most affected CI/CD platform with 1,064 exposed organizations, followed by GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, Jenkins, Bitbucket Pipelines, and CircleCI.
  • The stolen credentials included JWTs, private key blocks, AWS access keys, GitLab and GitHub personal access tokens, OpenAI keys, Slack webhooks, and Google API keys.
  • The article says Team PCP’s playbook is to compromise a trusted open source component, run a credential stealer in CI/CD pipelines, exfiltrate secrets over outbound network connections, and use stolen credentials to compromise the next target.

Technologies: ci-cd, source-control, package-registry, cloud-platform, siem

Products: harden-runner, secure-registry, github-checks, workflow-run-policies, threat-center, trivy-github-action, checkmarx-kics-action, telnyx-pypi-package, litellm, axios, github-actions, gitlab, azure-devops, jenkins, bitbucket-pipelines, circleci, openai-api

Vendors: stepsecurity, cloudsek, github, gitlab, microsoft, jenkins-project, atlassian, circleci, aquasecurity, checkmarx, telnyx, litellm, axios, openai, amazon-web-services, slack, google

New Mirai variant adds stealth capabilities to notorious botnet code — Must Read

FortiGuard Labs reports a new Mirai-based botnet, Evooo1Bot, is exploiting unpatched internet-facing routers and other edge devices from several vendors. Unlike typical Mirai variants, it adds stealthier encrypted command-and-control, honeypot avoidance, credential sniffing, and SOCKS proxy features that let attackers hide their origin and pivot through victims’ infrastructure.

  • FortiGuard Labs researchers said a previously undocumented Linux-based Mirai variant called Evooo1Bot has been actively exploiting vulnerabilities in internet-facing hardware for at least a month.
  • Evooo1Bot targets routers and other hardware from Alcatel, D-Link, Mitsubishi Electric, Netgear, Tenda and Telesquare.
  • FortiGuard Labs telemetry shows Evooo1Bot activity concentrated in North America, South America, Europe, India, China and Japan, but the report does not specify how many devices have been compromised.
  • Beyond Mirai’s usual distributed denial-of-service functions, Evooo1Bot includes encrypted command-and-control communications, an SSH scanner that avoids apparent honeypots, and a sniffer for unchanged default access credentials.
  • FortiGuard Labs said Evooo1Bot’s SOCKS proxy capability can turn compromised routers, firewalls, IP cameras and other edge devices into persistent proxies that help attackers conceal their origin and conduct follow-on operations through victims’ infrastructure.

Technologies: router, firewall, iot-device, proxy

Vendors: fortinet, alcatel, d-link, mitsubishi-electric, netgear, tenda, telesquare

Trezor discloses data breach affecting nearly 14,000 customers — Must Read

Trezor says nearly 14,000 customers had order contact details exposed after shipping provider ShipMonk was hacked through a Metabase zero-day. Trezor says its own systems and devices were not compromised, but affected customers should watch for targeted phishing attempts.

  • Trezor disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 14,000 customers after its shipping and logistics provider ShipMonk was hacked.
  • The exposed order data included full names, shipping addresses, email addresses, and phone numbers for 11,742 customers, while 1,947 customers had partial exposure of name, city, and email.
  • The breach affects customers from the United States, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Colombia, Brazil, Italy, and Portugal who received orders between May 10 and August 8, 2026.
  • Trezor said its own systems were not compromised, its operations and services were not impacted, and all Trezor devices remain secure.
  • ShipMonk told affected customers that attackers exploited a vulnerability in the third-party analytics platform Metabase, which Metabase said was a critical SQL injection zero-day used to access customer instances and steal data.

Products: metabase, trezor-hardware-wallet

Vendors: trezor, shipmonk, metabase

Microsoft patches LegacyHive Windows zero-day vulnerability — Should Read

Microsoft has patched the Windows LegacyHive zero-day, now tracked as CVE-2026-62832, which could let an authenticated local attacker with another account’s credentials load another user’s registry hive and gain administrator privileges. Organizations should apply the August Patch Tuesday updates to mitigate the flaw.

  • Microsoft released security patches for the Windows zero-day vulnerability known as LegacyHive as part of its August Patch Tuesday updates.
  • Microsoft now tracks LegacyHive as CVE-2026-62832 and says it stems from improper link resolution before file access in the Windows User Profile Service.
  • Microsoft says an authenticated attacker with credentials for another local account could run a specially crafted application to load another user’s registry hive, access or modify that user’s data, and gain administrator privileges.
  • The LegacyHive proof-of-concept exploit was published by a researcher using the handle Nightmare Eclipse hours after the July 2026 Patch Tuesday updates were released.
  • ACROS Security released free unofficial LegacyHive patches on July 20 for systems running Windows 10 2004 or later and Windows Server 2022 or later.

Technologies: operating-system, edr

Products: windows, windows-user-profile-service, microsoft-defender-for-endpoint, 0patch, windows-10, windows-server-2022

Vendors: microsoft, acros-security

Flock tightens privacy controls amid scandals over officer abuse — Should Read

Flock Safety is tightening controls on its license plate reader system after reports that police officers used it to stalk or track people for personal reasons. Critics say the changes may not prevent abuse because officers can still potentially misrepresent why they are running searches.

  • Flock Safety announced it will expand its “Audit Assistance” feature to all customers by the end of the year, with user accounts automatically suspended while abnormal activity is reviewed.
  • Flock will require officers to enter case codes tied to investigations when conducting searches, though the requirement can be bypassed in emergencies.
  • The policy changes follow reports that law enforcement officers used Flock license plate readers to track people for personal reasons, including alleged stalking cases in Massachusetts and Georgia.
  • ACLU senior policy counsel Chad Marlow criticized Flock’s announcement as largely a public relations move and said some measures repeat previously inadequate safeguards.
  • Flock said customers can limit when camera data is shared with other agencies, such as allowing searches for missing person cases but not for immigration enforcement.

Technologies: iot-device

Products: flock-license-plate-readers, audit-assistance

Vendors: flock-safety

When read-only mounts in Docker Sandboxes become writable — May Read

Docker Sandboxes versions 0.35.0 through 0.37.1 allowed read-only host mounts to be modified via a writable /mnt/host VirtioFS path, undermining sandbox file protections. Docker fixed the issue in version 0.38.0 and assigned it CVE-2026-18171.

  • Docker Sandboxes versions 0.35.0 through 0.37.1 had an issue where a directory mounted as read-only could still be written through another path.
  • The issue occurred because the same host directory was available both at the intended read-only mount point and through Docker's writable host export under /mnt/host.
  • A proof of concept showed that writing to /readonly/file.txt failed with a read-only file system error, but writing to /mnt/host/c/donotchangeme/file.txt changed the host file successfully.
  • The potential impact depended on what was mounted into the sandbox, such as source code, CI configuration, infrastructure code, application configuration, or build inputs.
  • Docker fixed the issue in Docker Sandboxes 0.38.0 and assigned it CVE-2026-18171 with a CVSS score of 5.7.

Technologies: container-platform, hypervisor

Products: docker-sandboxes, docker-engine, virtiofs

Vendors: docker

Attack of The Extensions — May Read

The article shows how Chromium profile modification can silently sideload browser extensions, Isolated Web Apps, and Native Messaging Hosts to turn Chrome or Edge into a persistent C2 foothold for cookie theft, OS interaction, and SOCKS-style pivoting. The key defensive takeaway is to monitor unusual browser profile and native messaging changes and enforce policies that disable extension developer mode.

  • The article introduces SilentChrome-BOF, a Beacon object file that modifies Chromium browser profile settings to install unpacked extensions, Isolated Web Applications, and Native Messaging Hosts.
  • The proof-of-concept Mythic agent Ditto runs as a Chromium extension and can collect cookies, enumerate tabs, capture pages, query browser history, and communicate with optional sidecar components.
  • SilentChrome-BOF installs an unpacked extension by editing the Secure Preferences file, adding extension state, enabling developer mode, recalculating legacy preference MACs, removing encrypted hash entries, and recalculating the super_mac.
  • Ditto can use an Isolated Web Application with Direct Sockets for SOCKS-style pivoting and a Native Messaging Host to interact with the Windows operating system through a local executable.
  • The article recommends detecting this technique by monitoring changes to Chromium Preferences and Secure Preferences files, Native Messaging Host registry keys, IWA-related Chrome process arguments, and native messaging process creation events.

Technologies: browser, operating-system

Products: chromium, google-chrome, microsoft-edge, microsoft-windows, silentchrome-bof, ditto, mythic, sysmon

Vendors: google, microsoft, chromium-project, mythic-project

Return of the Cookie Monster — May Read

The article shows that even with Chrome’s newer cookie protections, attackers can still enable the Chrome DevTools Protocol inside a running Chrome or Edge session to steal browser data or take over authenticated browsing. Defenders should monitor for signs of process injection into Chromium browsers, such as suspicious remote thread creation and process access events.

  • Chrome 136 changed remote debugging behavior so that --remote-debugging-port or --remote-debugging-pipe is ignored for the default profile unless paired with a non-standard --user-data-dir, which prevents immediate access to the user’s normal cookies, extensions, and browser state when launching a new browser with CDP enabled.
  • CDP-Enable-BOF enables the Chrome DevTools Protocol from inside a live chrome.exe or msedge.exe process by locating browser internals, installing a remote window procedure, and calling Chromium’s internal StartRemoteDebuggingServer on a requested port.
  • Once CDP is enabled in a running Chromium browser, CDP-Toolkit can enumerate tabs, dump cookies, search history, capture screenshots, list bookmarks and extensions, extract saved password information, and support browser takeover workflows.
  • The BOF depends on masked signatures for internal Chromium symbols such as StartRemoteDebuggingServer, operator new, TCPServerSocketFactory::CreateForHttpServer, and TCPServerSocketFactory, which may need to be updated when Chrome or Edge changes.
  • The article’s detection section highlights Sysmon Event IDs 8 and 10, especially CreateRemoteThread activity targeting chrome.exe or msedge.exe combined with ProcessAccess showing Granted Access 0x143a, as possible indicators of browser process injection.

Technologies: browser, operating-system

Products: google-chrome, microsoft-edge, chromium, chrome-devtools-protocol, cdp-enable-bof, cdp-toolkit, sysmon, sysmon-modular

Vendors: google, microsoft, chromium-project, specterops

AI 'watermark removers' flood the web. Almost none can prove they work. — May Read

A wave of tools claiming to remove Anthropic Claude’s new invisible AI text watermark has appeared, but almost none can prove they work because Anthropic has not released its detector or technical details. Most tools only strip metadata or hidden characters, while removing the real word-choice watermark likely requires heavy rewriting and creates a new supply-chain risk as users wire unvetted tools into AI workflows.

  • A market for AI watermark removal tools appeared shortly after Anthropic disclosed that Claude now adds invisible marks to everything it writes or processes.
  • Claims that tools can defeat Anthropic’s text watermark cannot currently be verified because Anthropic has not published how the watermark works or released a detector.
  • Some tools can remove hidden characters and file metadata, but the article says Claude’s watermark is embedded in the model’s word choices rather than in hidden characters.
  • Guillaume Meyer said his watermarks-remover tool currently removes metadata only and does not yet strip the actual text watermark.
  • The article warns that people wiring unvetted watermark-removal tools into agent workflows and feeding documents through them creates a supply chain risk.

Technologies: source-control, cloud-platform

Products: claude, watermarks-remover, claude-watermark-cleaner, remove-ai-watermarks, noai-watermark, gemini, synthid-text, claude-code, claude-cowork, claude-tag, microsoft-foundry, github

Vendors: anthropic, google, openai, stealthgpt, human-writes, github, microsoft, amazon-web-services

Who Vets AI’s Code? The Scale Challenge Facing Open Source Ingestion — Optional

AI coding assistants can introduce hallucinated or unvetted open source dependencies faster than traditional security reviews can catch them, creating slopsquatting and supply-chain risks. The article argues organizations should vet and control packages at the point of selection through curated ingestion gateways rather than relying only on post-commit scans.

  • The article argues that AI coding assistants can suggest third-party dependencies faster than traditional post-commit Software Composition Analysis scans can review them.
  • The article describes slopsquatting as a supply-chain risk where an AI model suggests a nonexistent package name, an attacker registers that name on PyPI or npm with a malicious payload, and developer or CI/CD systems later fetch it.
  • The article cites a USENIX Security study of sixteen code-generation models across more than 500,000 code samples that found some AI-suggested package names did not exist in public registries and nearly half of resolving dependencies had known CVEs or outdated releases.
  • The article says automated AI-generated pull requests are increasing review pressure on open source maintainers, while projects such as Kubernetes, the Linux kernel, LLVM, and Godot have published differing policies on AI-assisted contributions.
  • The article recommends blocking direct public registry fetching, isolating AI-suggested dependencies for analysis, and using a governed ingestion gateway so packages are vetted before they reach builds.

Technologies: package-registry, ci-cd, source-control, orchestration, operating-system

Products: activestate-secure-open-source-library, activestate-curated-catalog, pypi, npm, kubernetes, linux-kernel, llvm, godot, react-codeshift

Vendors: activestate, python-software-foundation, npm, kubernetes, linux-foundation, llvm, godot, coderabbit, kusari

item.title: FortiWeb CVE-2026-26035, SCCM RCE Chain, and U.S. Hack-Back Plan Lead Digest
item.content:encoded:
Window: 13 Aug 10:00 → 13 Aug 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Potential for Remote Code Execution in Microsoft SCCM via Newly-Discovered Exploit Chain — Should Read

XM Cyber researchers found an SCCM exploit chain that can let a low-privileged domain user or certain SCCM operators gain remote code execution as SYSTEM on the primary site server, potentially compromising the whole environment. Microsoft has patched only the initial RBAC bypass, so organizations should restrict AdminService access and audit SCCM roles until the remaining fixes arrive.

  • XM Cyber researchers discovered a chain of vulnerabilities in Microsoft System Center Configuration Management that could allow remote code execution by a standard domain user with no SCCM permissions, no admin role, and no user interaction.
  • The exploit chain targets the SCCM primary site server and combines a missing authorization check in an AdminService upload endpoint, a CabSlip path traversal issue, weak code-signing verification, and privileged DLL loading by SMS Executive.
  • Microsoft assigned CVE-2026-47301 to one of the reported vulnerabilities and released a fix for the broken authorization issue in July 2026, but the rest of the chain remains unpatched until a planned ConfigMgr 2609 release in October 2026.
  • Users assigned the built-in Operations Administrator role, or any custom role with Create permission on the SMS_ConsoleExtensionData object type, can still trigger the downstream exploit chain through a different API.
  • The article recommends monitoring AdminService.log for System.IO.DirectoryNotFoundException followed by HTTP 500 errors, watching for unexpected changes to adsource.dll, restricting network access to the AdminService API port, and auditing SCCM role assignments.

Products: microsoft-system-center-configuration-manager, adminservice, sms-executive

Vendors: microsoft, xm-cyber

$7 Million in Expired Domains Fuel a Streaming Empire with a Malware Secret — Should Read

Infoblox says the Sable Squirrel threat actor has spent an estimated $7 million buying expired, trusted domains to run a large illegal sports streaming and gambling network. Some of the same domains also serve as command-and-control infrastructure for RAT malware and ransomware-linked samples, showing the operation monetizes its domain empire through both gambling traffic and malware.

  • Infoblox Threat Intel says Sable Squirrel controls more than 10,000 domains used for illegal sports streaming, online gambling promotion, traffic redirection, CDN and tracking infrastructure, mobile app distribution, and malware command-and-control.
  • Infoblox confirmed more than $430,000 in dropcatch purchases across roughly 160 domains and estimates Sable Squirrel’s total dropcatch spend is north of $7 million.
  • Researchers identified over 31,000 malware samples connecting to Sable Squirrel domains, including Quasar RAT, AsyncRAT, DCRat, NanoCore, Remcos, njRAT, and samples carrying HiddenTear ransomware signatures.
  • A coordinated wave in late 2025 configured hundreds of existing Sable Squirrel domains as malware command-and-control while many of those domains continued presenting live football streaming content to visitors.
  • Vietnamese enforcement actions in February and March 2026 froze flagship sites, charged 30 suspects, and seized roughly 300 billion VND, but Infoblox observed that registrations recovered within a month and the operation expanded toward the 2026 World Cup.

Technologies: cms, remote-access

Products: wordpress, google-play, cloudflare-nameservers, dropcatch.com, keitaro, quasar-rat, asyncrat, dcrat, nanocore, remcos, njrat, hiddentear

Vendors: infoblox, wordpress, google, cloudflare, godaddy, dropcatch, namecheap, dynadot, thesports, aiscore, keitaro, bropush

Dropcatch Scavengers: Expired Malicious Domains Become Cash Cows — Should Read

Infoblox found that multiple threat actors are buying expired malicious domains still embedded in compromised websites, then reusing the inherited traffic to push scams, ad fraud, and malware. The key risk is that old website compromises continue harming visitors even after the original attacker’s domains expire, because dropcatch actors can easily take over the abandoned infrastructure.

  • Infoblox reports that some threat actors acquire expired malicious domains still embedded in compromised websites and use the inherited traffic to redirect visitors to scams, unwanted content, affiliate advertising, or malware.
  • Stuffy Squirrel has operated since at least 2020, controls over 500 domains, hides malicious activity inside legitimate-looking scripts, and monetizes traffic through affiliate advertising platforms such as ExoClick and PushHouse.
  • Shady Squirrel has operated since at least July 2023, has acquired over 700 domains, and in 2026 sent traffic to 1Win, a tech support scam actor, SocGholish, and a Keitaro server.
  • Infoblox says Shady Squirrel helped SocGholish regain access to tens of thousands of compromised sites about 10 days after Operation Endgame disrupted SocGholish infrastructure in June 2026.
  • Swiping Squirrel has acquired over 3,000 domains since 2022 and sells traffic mainly to Team Internet’s ZeroPark, where visitors may be routed to malware, scams, or commerce pages.

Technologies: cms, cloud-platform

Products: keitaro, binom, zeropark, propush, exoclick, pushhouse, azure-static-web-apps, raphael-js, wordpress, magento, aliexpress, kelkoo

Vendors: infoblox, microsoft, team-internet, propeller-ads, exoclick, pushhouse, aliexpress, kelkoo, sucuri, zscaler

Dissecting the JWR phishing framework — Should Read

Cisco Talos analyzed JWR, a sophisticated real-time phishing framework likely related to The Outsider PhaaS, that lets operators live-control victim sessions and steal payment data, credentials, identity documents, 2FA codes, and device fingerprints. Talos observed it being delivered through SMS lures impersonating toll, postal, and courier services across Southeast Asia and the Middle East.

  • Cisco Talos identified an undocumented phishing framework internally branded “JWR” that impersonates checkout and login pages for major payment and shopping platforms.
  • The JWR client engine keeps an AES-CTR encrypted WebSocket open to the threat actor, allowing the operator to steer each victim’s session live instead of only collecting submitted form data.
  • JWR targets payment data, identity documents, Social Security numbers, passport and driver’s license images, website and PayPal credentials, 2FA codes, and device fingerprints.
  • Talos assesses with medium confidence that JWR is a variant of “The Outsider” phishing-as-a-service platform based on similarities in client engine scripts and functionality.
  • Talos observed a real-world SMS phishing campaign delivering the JWR client through lures impersonating toll authorities, postal services, and courier services in Southeast Asia and the Middle East.

Technologies: cms, antivirus, ids-ips

Products: jwr-phishing-framework, the-outsider, shopify, paypal, apple-id, klarna, woocommerce, vue.js, clamav, snort

Vendors: cisco-talos, shopify, paypal, apple, klarna, woocommerce, vuejs

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-26035) FortiWeb Admin Authentication Bypass via RADIUS Admin Groups — Should Read

Fortinet disclosed CVE-2026-26035, a FortiWeb authentication bypass that can let unauthenticated attackers gain admin access when RADIUS-based admin groups are configured. Organizations should urgently identify FortiWeb appliances using RADIUS admin authentication, restrict management access, audit for suspicious logins, and confirm fixed versions with Fortinet.

  • CVE-2026-26035 is an improper authentication vulnerability in Fortinet FortiWeb’s remote RADIUS administrator authentication path, disclosed by Fortinet on August 12, 2026 in advisory FG-IR-26-158.
  • Public reporting states that a remote attacker with no valid credentials can log in to the FortiWeb GUI and CLI using arbitrary usernames and passwords and obtain administrative access to the appliance.
  • Fortinet lists the 8.0, 7.6, 7.4, 7.2, and 7.0 branches of FortiWeb as affected, with third-party trackers reporting specific vulnerable ranges across those branches.
  • The deployments at risk are FortiWeb appliances configured to authenticate administrators against a RADIUS server through an admin group, rather than every FortiWeb instance running an affected build.
  • Fortinet has published an advisory, but the article says defenders should confirm fixed versions directly with Fortinet because specific fixed build numbers could not be independently confirmed at the time of writing.

Technologies: waf

Products: fortiweb, cycognito-platform

Vendors: fortinet, cycognito

Trump taps cyber firms to go on offensive against criminals — Should Read

The Trump administration will allow vetted U.S. cybersecurity firms to conduct government-approved offensive cyber operations against transnational cybercrime groups under DOJ and DHS oversight. The plan aims to disrupt scams and ransomware but raises legal and safety concerns for participating companies and employees.

  • The Trump administration will allow vetted private U.S. companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against transnational cybercrime organizations in partnership with the Justice and Homeland Security departments.
  • DOJ and DHS officials must review and provide written approval for each cyber operations package before a participating company can take action.
  • The presidential memorandum says officials will not approve operations that result in loss of life or rise to the level of use of force or armed attack under international law.
  • Participating companies will sign contracts, undergo rigorous vetting, report activities routinely to the federal government, and face penalties of at least $1 million for violations.
  • Cybersecurity experts raised concerns about unclear legal protections, possible foreign government targeting of participating employees, and protocols for mistakes or misidentified targets.

The State of Ransomware Q2 2026 — Should Read

Check Point Research reports that ransomware activity stayed near record highs in Q2 2026, with more active groups emerging even as leaders like Qilin and The Gentlemen still dominated victim counts. The report also highlights falling ransom payment rates, faster AI-assisted tooling and exploit development, and law enforcement efforts targeting shared criminal infrastructure.

  • Check Point Research reported that the top 10 ransomware groups accounted for 57.6% of victims in Q2 2026, down from 71% in Q1, while the number of active groups rose from 71 to 93.
  • Data leak sites recorded 2,139 ransomware victims in Q2 2026, which was essentially flat compared with Q1 and 33% higher year over year.
  • Qilin remained the most prolific ransomware operator for a fourth straight quarter with 279 victims, while The Gentlemen rose 62% to 269 victims and outpaced Qilin during June.
  • An internal leak of The Gentlemen exposed a core team of roughly nine operators, a broader affiliate base, and evidence that the group used AI coding assistants to build its ransomware management panel in about three days.
  • Ransom payment rates fell to a multi-year low near 23%, even as on-chain ransomware payments still exceeded $820 million in 2025.

Vendors: check-point-research

Germany moves to give spy agencies hacking and sabotage powers — Should Read

Germany’s cabinet approved a major intelligence reform bill that would give its spy agencies new powers to hack foreign systems, disrupt hostile infrastructure, sabotage supply chains, and conduct limited domestic operational interference. The proposal includes safeguards and AI-analysis rules but is expected to face civil liberties challenges.

  • Germany’s cabinet approved legislation that would allow its intelligence agencies to hack foreign systems, sabotage adversaries’ supply chains, and feed false information to extremists inside Germany.
  • The draft bill rewrites the laws governing Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, and its domestic agency for the protection of the constitutional order, the BfV.
  • The bill would require telecommunications carriers and digital service providers to assist the agencies, with enforcement powers that could result in fines or service suspensions.
  • The proposed powers bar intelligence agencies from measures intended to endanger a person’s life or physical safety.
  • The bill authorizes intelligence agencies to use self-learning systems for analysis, prohibits discriminatory algorithms, and requires machine-generated outputs to be spot-checked under qualified supervision.

One Extra Letter, Full Auth Pass, Nothing to Scan — Should Read

Attackers used a one-letter typosquatted vendor domain with properly configured SPF, DKIM and DMARC to send an ACH payment-change request that passed authentication and contained no malicious links or payloads. The key lesson is that email authentication proves domain control, not legitimacy, so payment changes must be verified outside email and checked against trusted vendor records.

  • A large U.S. regional healthcare system received an ACH enrolment notice that appeared to come from Arthrex, a medical-device manufacturer it already did business with.
  • The attacker used the typosquatted domain arthrrex.com, which differs from the legitimate arthrex.com domain by a doubled “r”.
  • The message passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, Microsoft composite authentication, and ARC checks because the attacker owned and correctly configured the sending domain.
  • The email and attached PDF contained no malicious links, JavaScript, form fields, executable content, account numbers, or routing details for scanners to evaluate.
  • IRONSCALES Themis scored the message at 84 percent confidence based on the newly registered return-path domain, and four mailboxes across two waves in mid-July were quarantined and mitigated.

Technologies: email-security

Products: themis, microsoft-word, microsoft-365

Vendors: ironscales, microsoft

Brazil orders Discord to suspend livestreaming after teen suicide — Should Read

Brazil ordered Discord to suspend its Go Live livestreaming feature nationwide after authorities said a 13-year-old was encouraged to die by suicide during a broadcast and regulators found evidence of child-safety failures. Discord said it is reviewing the order and called the suspension premature.

  • Brazil’s National Data Protection Authority ordered Discord to suspend its Go Live livestreaming feature in Brazil until the company can show it has effective safeguards to protect children and teenagers.
  • The order follows the death of a 13-year-old girl in central-western Brazil whom authorities say was encouraged to harm herself during a roughly 45-minute Discord livestream in July.
  • Brazilian authorities said five teenagers have been arrested in connection with the case and that police intervened in a separate incident involving a girl preparing to die by suicide during an online broadcast.
  • The ANPD said it found robust evidence that Discord failed to take reasonable steps to protect children and teenagers from harmful content promoting or facilitating violence, self-harm, or suicide.
  • Discord confirmed it had received the order, said it was reviewing it, and called the suspension of livestreaming in Brazil premature.

Products: discord, go-live, telegram

Vendors: discord, telegram

WhatsApp rolls out new feature that flags potential scam messages — May Read

WhatsApp is rolling out an optional Scam Alert feature that uses on-device machine learning to warn users about likely scam messages from non-contacts without sending message content to Meta. Users can block, report, continue, or mark chats as trusted, with optional sharing of recent messages to improve accuracy.

  • WhatsApp has begun a limited beta rollout of an optional Scam Alert feature that uses an on-device machine learning model to warn users about potential scam messages.
  • Scam Alert checks incoming messages from non-contacts against known scam patterns using linguistic signals and the structure of the conversation.
  • When Scam Alert detects a potential scam attempt, it shows a chat warning asking the user to block, report, or continue the conversation.
  • WhatsApp says no message content leaves the device for classification or is automatically reported to WhatsApp, Meta, or anyone else.
  • Users can mark a flagged chat as trusted to stop future Scam Alert warnings for that chat, and they can optionally share the last five received messages with WhatsApp to help improve the feature.

Products: whatsapp, scam-alert, strict-account-settings

Vendors: meta, whatsapp

Drop Something? Don’t Worry, Someone Caught it — May Read

Infoblox found that about one in five newly registered domains are previously expired domains that have been re-registered, giving them inherited reputation, traffic, and lingering connections that can be abused. Defenders should treat dropped domains as a security risk because ownership changes can transfer trust to domain investors or threat actors.

  • Infoblox observed over 50,000 dropcatch domains per day in gTLDs during the first half of 2026, rising to around 65,000 per day when various ccTLDs were included.
  • Nearly 20% of observed gTLD registrations were dropcatch domains, meaning about one in five newly registered domains had a prior registration history.

Plug and Pwn attack uses fake USB devices for Windows SYSTEM access — Should Read

Researchers showed that Windows Plug and Play can be abused with fake USB devices, or even RDP USB redirection, to make Windows install vulnerable vendor software and gain SYSTEM privileges. Disabling co-installers helps against some chains, but sensitive environments should also restrict device installation and disable unnecessary PnP redirection.

  • Security researchers Alejandro Hernando and Borja Martínez disclosed “Plug and Pwn” attacks that abuse Windows Plug and Play to make Windows install vulnerable or insecure vendor software and gain NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges.
  • The researchers used FaceDancer with Cynthion and GreatFET hardware to emulate USB devices, causing Windows to recognize the fake hardware and install associated vendor driver packages.
  • One demonstrated zero-click physical attack impersonated Sierra Wireless and Sony FeliCa devices against a fully updated Windows 11 computer with nobody logged in, taking approximately five minutes to obtain a SYSTEM reverse shell.
  • The researchers also demonstrated “NoPlug & Pwn,” which abuses RDP USB redirection with a Python RDP client to make a remote Windows host enumerate a fake USB device and install driver software as SYSTEM.
  • Setting the DisableCoInstallers registry value can disrupt some demonstrated attacks, but Hernando said it does not stop the broader attack class because Plug and Play enumeration, Windows Update resolution, driver staging, INF processing, and INF-installed services remain exposed.

Defenders should disable WS-Trust/usernamemixed or block legacy authentication and monitor Unified Audit Logs for autologon activity.

  • The article describes how Microsoft Entra ID’s legacy WS-Trust autologon endpoint for Seamless SSO can accept direct username and password requests from the internet.
  • Testing found that password spray attempts through the autologon endpoint bypassed Smart Lockout, with more than 1,000 failed attempts against one account from a single unfamiliar IP without receiving a locked-account response.
  • Failed authentication attempts against the autologon endpoint did not appear in standard Entra ID sign-in logs, though the article says the Unified Audit Log can capture requests to autologon.microsoftazuread-sso.com.
  • The endpoint returns different AADSTS error codes that can distinguish wrong passwords from valid passwords blocked later by MFA, Conditional Access, or password-expiration requirements.
  • The article recommends disabling the usernamemixed endpoint, blocking legacy authentication through Conditional Access, enabling Unified Audit Log alerts for autologon requests, and moving accounts toward passwordless sign-in methods.

The UK’s ACRO Criminal Records Office was reprimanded after three intrusions went undetected for nearly two years, enabled by an unpatched Kentico portal and ignored security alerts. Attackers staged sensitive data on nearly 11,000 people for possible theft, though poor logging meant ACRO could not confirm whether it was exfiltrated.

  • The UK Information Commissioner’s Office reprimanded ACRO Criminal Records Office after three separate intrusions between July 2021 and June 2023 exposed personal data belonging to thousands of people, including victims of domestic violence.
  • All three attacks exploited ACRO’s public-facing customer portal, which used a Kentico content management system that had not been patched since September 2019 despite known vulnerabilities.
  • ACRO’s Trend Micro security system generated numerous warnings during the attack period, including detections of attempts to install Mimikatz, but the alerts were not acted upon.

The key takeaway is that organizations are logging more activity but still failing to block or alert on the stealthy actions attackers use before launching noisier attacks.

  • Picus Labs’ Blue Report 2026 measured more than 338 million real attack simulations across client production environments in the first half of 2026 and found average prevention effectiveness rose from 62% to 69%.
  • For the first time, Picus Labs measured post-compromise prevention with autonomous penetration testing and found a Post-Compromise Prevention Rate of 37%.
  • Inside networks, defenses stopped noisy actions such as lateral movement through service execution around 90% of the time, but stopped reconnaissance only 10% of the time and one registry-based credential-theft variant in less than 1% of attempts.
  • The report found that logging reached a four-year high of 58%, while the alert score stayed at 14%, meaning fewer than one in seven simulated attacks produced an alert.

The system uses checks by users, contacts, and third-party auditors Cloudflare and Trail of Bits to detect malicious key swaps.

  • Signal introduced Automatic Key Verification, a new security feature designed to help users ensure their encrypted chats have not been intercepted.
  • Automatic Key Verification is part of a key transparency system that uses Cloudflare and Trail of Bits as trusted third-party independent auditors to verify the integrity of Signal conversations.
  • Signal says the system checks that the association between a phone number or username and its public encryption key is globally consistent and transparent across Signal’s ecosystem.
  • Users can enable Automatic Key Verification in Signal under Settings, Privacy, Advanced, or use the “Verify Automatically” option on the safety number verification screen.

Two Brands in One Message, One URL Built at Runtime — May Read

A phishing email disguised as a DocuSign remittance notice used a clean-scanning HTML attachment to impersonate Microsoft SharePoint and build its credential-harvesting redirect only after the victim submitted a form. The key lesson is that messages with no visible links and benign file verdicts can still hide phishing logic that runs client-side after user interaction.

  • A shared remittance mailbox at a medical device manufacturer received an unauthenticated email styled as a DocuSign notice about a completed payment document.
  • The email’s visible call-to-action pointed to an empty anchor, while the real lure was a 16,462-byte HTML attachment that the file scanner marked clean.
  • Opening the attachment displayed a fake Microsoft SharePoint secure access page with a locked document label and a form asking the recipient to enter a work address.
  • The attachment’s inline script built the destination URL only after form submission, using Google redirect endpoints and a base64-encoded recipient address in the fragment.
  • Adaptive AI labeled the message as invoice phishing with 90 confidence, and the incident record said it was automatically resolved as phishing.

StepSecurity argues that organizations migrating away from public package registries need visibility across both CI jobs and developer machines, because either can still silently fetch dependencies from npm, PyPI, Docker Hub, or other public sources. Its controls are positioned to detect and help enforce use of internal or secure registries so malicious or compromised packages are blocked before installation.

  • Many engineering organizations are moving package downloads away from public registries and behind internal registries so policies like cooldown periods and compromised package blocking apply before packages are installed.
  • StepSecurity says internal registries cannot show jobs or developer machines that bypass them, because they only log requests that reach the internal registry.
  • The Harden Runner control for CI jobs passes when a job’s network baseline contains no calls to public package registries such as registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org, or registry-1.docker.io.
  • The Dev Machine Guard control for developer machines reads package manager configuration files such as .npmrc and pip.conf to report the effective registry and where that value came from.
  • The article recommends blocking public registries at the network level in CI, centrally setting registry configuration on developer machines, and applying download-time policies at the registry itself.

Finding vulnerabilities at every stage: what to run, and when — Optional

The article argues that SAST, Deep PR Review, AI Code Analysis, and AI Pentesting are complementary layers, not replacements for one another. Together they cover vulnerabilities from early code changes through live exploit validation, with each tool best suited to a different stage of the development lifecycle.

  • The article describes four different approaches to finding application vulnerabilities: traditional SAST, Deep PR Review, AI Code Analysis, and AI Pentesting.
  • Traditional SAST is deterministic and cheap enough to run on every commit or pull request, but it only checks for known code patterns and cannot reason about application logic.
  • Deep PR Review examines each pull request in the context of the wider repository to catch business logic issues such as IDORs and broken access control before code merges.
  • AI Code Analysis applies similar reasoning across an entire repository without needing a live environment, making it useful for major changes, full releases, and hard-to-test targets.
  • AI Pentesting runs against a live application to attempt real exploitation, providing evidence of exploitability and satisfying live penetration test requirements for frameworks such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001.

Attackers are actively exploiting a critical VMware vCenter directory-traversal flaw, CVE-2026-59310, to compromise servers and install reverse_ssh for persistent remote access. Organizations should urgently patch vCenter and investigate unexpected outbound SSH-related connections or unauthorized cron jobs on appliances.

  • Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2026-59310, a critical directory-traversal vulnerability in Broadcom VMware vCenter with a CVSS score of 9.8.

  • Compromised systems identified by QUIRSO first contacted attacker domains on August 3, five days after Broadcom publicly disclosed the flaws.

Cisco ASA and FTD devices with Remote Access SSL VPN-related services exposed are vulnerable to unauthenticated denial-of-service attacks under CVE-2026-20349, which is already being exploited. Cisco has released hot fixes and says there are no workarounds, so affected internet-facing firewalls and VPN gateways should be patched urgently.

  • CVE-2026-20349 is a denial of service vulnerability in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software and Cisco Secure Firewall FTD Software caused by insufficient error checking when processing HTTP requests.
  • The vulnerability has a CVSS v3.1 base score of 8.6, requires no authentication or user interaction, and can allow an attacker with network access to send a crafted HTTP request that causes the device to reload unexpectedly.
  • Cisco said its Product Security Incident Response Team became aware of active exploitation in August 2026, and CISA added CVE-2026-20349 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on August 11, 2026.
  • Affected devices are vulnerable releases of Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software or Cisco Secure FTD Software with SSL VPN, IKEv2 remote access VPN with client services, or Zero Trust Network Access enabled, while Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center Software is not affected.
  • Cisco has released hot fixes for affected ASA and FTD releases and states that there are no workarounds, making upgrade to a fixed release the only remediation.

A researcher released ShieldBreak, a proof-of-concept zero-day claiming to bypass Microsoft’s patch for the Defender RoguePlanet privilege-escalation flaw and gain SYSTEM access on current Windows versions. Microsoft has been contacted as concerns grow around recent Windows privilege-escalation vulnerabilities and patch effectiveness.

CVE-2026-10579 is a critical pre-authentication bypass in Red Hat JBoss EAP’s PicketLink SAML handling that can let attackers forge identities and gain unauthorized access, potentially as administrators. No fix is available yet, so organizations should inventory exposed PicketLink deployments, restrict SAML endpoints, and disable unsolicited response handling where possible.

  • Red Hat lists Red Hat JBoss Enterprise Application Platform 7 and Red Hat JBoss Enterprise Application Platform 8 as affected products, but the advisory did not name specific vulnerable or fixed version ranges at the time of writing.

CVE-2026-72766 is a high-severity n8n Send Email node flaw that can let attackers read local files or perform SSRF when exposed unauthenticated webhooks pass untrusted input into email body fields. Organizations should upgrade to fixed n8n versions and audit externally reachable instances and workflows for risky Send Email configurations.

  • CVE-2026-72766 is a type confusion vulnerability in the Send Email node of n8n that can cause Nodemailer to interpret non-string workflow input as a file path or URL instead of message text.
  • Exploitation requires an active unauthenticated webhook, valid SMTP credentials configured on the Send Email node, and untrusted input mapped directly into the text or html body field, which n8n states is not a default configuration.

  • The vulnerability affects n8n versions before 1.123.67, 2.x versions before 2.31.5, and 2.32.x versions before 2.32.1, with patches available in those fixed releases.

Courier fraud in the UK exceeded £21 million in losses in 2025, with over-70s heavily targeted as criminals shift to WhatsApp contact, third-party couriers, and high-value goods like gold and jewellery. AI governance must include identity intelligence for every human, machine, service account, pipeline, and autonomous agent that can influence AI decisions or actions. Without clear attribution, delegated authority controls, and continuous trust checks, organizations may secure the model while leaving the identities around it dangerously ungoverned.

  • Agentic AI systems need their own governed identities with privileges limited by task, resource, duration, context, and risk, rather than inheriting a user’s full access or relying on shared credentials.

AI governance must include identity intelligence for every human, machine, service account, pipeline, and autonomous agent that can influence AI decisions or actions. Without clear attribution, delegated authority controls, and continuous trust checks, organizations may secure the model while leaving the identities around it dangerously ungoverned.

  • The article argues that AI governance must include the identities that build, train, deploy, modify, invoke, and oversee AI systems, not only models, data, and outputs.
  • Identity intelligence can help fraud and risk models determine who is behind suspicious activity and whether related accounts, devices, phone numbers, credentials, or infrastructure are connected.
  • Industrial and operational AI systems rely heavily on machine identities such as sensors, gateways, controllers, robots, maintenance platforms, and analytics engines, where an identity failure can become an operational or physical safety failure.
  • Agentic AI systems need their own governed identities with privileges limited by task, resource, duration, context, and risk, rather than inheriting a user’s full access or relying on shared credentials.
  • The article says organizations should be able to identify who trained an AI system, who changed it, who approved it, what data it used, what authority it holds, who invoked it, and who can stop it.

The Human Risk Layer of AI — Optional

AI agents increasingly act like credentialed employees, accessing data, systems, and workflows, so securing them requires addressing human behavior and workforce risk in addition to technical controls. The paper argues that Human Risk Management helps close the gap between what AI systems can do and how employees will actually use them.

  • The article presents a white paper titled “The Human Risk Layer of AI,” dated August 12, 2026.
  • The paper argues that securing large language models requires more than technical controls and must address workforce behavior.
  • The article states that AI agents now share access, data, and decision authority with the people who deploy them.
  • AI agents can make calls to internal systems, generate code, send communications, summarize documents, and execute multi-step workflows on behalf of human operators.
  • The article says AI agents are indistinguishable from a workforce member with credentials for security purposes.

Cybersecurity in the Lab — Optional

Health-ISAC’s Phil Englert warns that laboratory environments face distinct cybersecurity risks that may be underrepresented in broader healthcare security plans. Labs should assess those risks and apply targeted protections for connected medical and diagnostic systems.

  • The article focuses on cybersecurity risks that are unique to laboratory environments compared to other healthcare settings.
  • Phil Englert, Health-ISAC Vice President of Medical Device Security, discusses three major risks that laboratories should be aware of.
  • Phil Englert also provides recommendations for laboratories in the related Medical Laboratory Observer article.

Control Which Package Registries Your CI Jobs and Developer Machines Use — Optional

StepSecurity argues that organizations moving package downloads behind internal registries need visibility across both CI jobs and developer machines, because either can still silently fall back to public registries. Its registry controls show where installs are actually resolving from so teams can enforce private registry use and reduce exposure to compromised packages.

  • Engineering organizations are moving package downloads away from public registries and behind internal registries so that policies such as cooldown periods and compromised package blocking can apply before packages are installed.
  • The article cites malicious versions of axios on npm, two litellm releases on PyPI with a credential stealer, and a republished @bitwarden/cli that stole credentials from a developer machine and used GitHub tokens to inject malicious workflows into CI.
  • StepSecurity says internal registries cannot show jobs or developer machines that bypass them, because they only log requests that reached the internal registry.
  • The “Jobs should use a secure registry instead of public package registries” control uses Harden Runner to monitor actual outbound network calls from CI jobs and fails when a job calls public registries such as registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org, or registry-1.docker.io.
  • The “Developer machines should use a secure registry instead of public package registries” control uses Dev Machine Guard to read package manager configuration files and report each device-and-tool pair’s effective registry and the source of that setting.

Microsoft Patch Tuesday for August 2026 — Snort rules and prominent vulnerabilities — Must Read

Microsoft’s August 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes 421 vulnerabilities, including 62 critical flaws and one Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock privilege escalation bug already exploited in the wild. Cisco Talos released new Snort rules to help detect exploitation attempts for selected vulnerabilities.

  • Microsoft’s August 2026 security update addresses 421 vulnerabilities across multiple products, including 62 marked as critical.
  • Microsoft stated that CVE-2026-68820, an elevation of privilege vulnerability in the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock, has been exploited in the wild.
  • Of the 62 critical vulnerabilities, 40 are remote code execution vulnerabilities.
  • Microsoft assessed exploitation as more likely for critical vulnerabilities affecting Windows Deployment Services TFTP Server, Microsoft SharePoint Server, and Windows DHCP Server.
  • Cisco Talos released a new Snort ruleset to detect attempts to exploit some of the disclosed vulnerabilities.

CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard Weaponizes Hotel Wi-Fi Captive Portals to Steal Microsoft 365 Credentials — Must Read

Microsoft says Russia-linked Midnight Blizzard is hijacking hotel and conference Wi-Fi captive portals to redirect travelers to fake Microsoft 365 login, device-code phishing, and malware pages. The campaign can bypass conventional MFA and deliver CornFlake and ChocoShell to steal credentials, tokens, and cloud access.

  • Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported an ongoing credential theft campaign called CaptiveCrunch and attributed it to Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard linked to Russia.
  • The campaign manipulates DNS and HTTP traffic on captive portal networks at hotels, conference centers, and similar venues to redirect victims to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
  • Victims are sent to fake Microsoft 365 sign-in pages, device code phishing pages abusing Microsoft Entra ID authentication, or fake browser and operating system update pages using the ClickFix technique.
  • The campaign delivers CornFlake, a Go-based Windows remote access trojan, and ChocoShell, an in-memory PowerShell information stealer that harvests browser credentials and Microsoft 365 and Azure AD/WAM tokens.
  • ReliaQuest identified compromised gateways in several U.S. cities, India, and Saudi Arabia, and the article says CaptiveCrunch has expanded to target Android devices through malicious APK files.

737 Chrome VPN Extensions Linked to Brand Impersonation and Browser Traffic Redirection — Should Read

Socket researchers found 737 Chrome VPN/proxy extensions, many impersonating trusted privacy brands, that route users’ entire browser traffic through SOCKS5 proxies controlled by a single Russian-linked Myxa VPN operation. The campaign targets Russian-speaking users seeking censorship circumvention and exposes their browsing activity while also using DNS-over-HTTPS evasion, fake premium servers, and Chrome Web Store policy evasion.

  • Socket’s Threat Research Team identified 737 free VPN and proxy extensions across at least 40 Chrome Web Store developer accounts, with 274 impersonating 66 established VPN and privacy brands.
  • Socket analyzed code from 522 retrieved extensions and found that 520 configured Chrome to route browser traffic through the same SOCKS5 proxy infrastructure on port 1082 with only loopback addresses in the bypass list.
  • The campaign accumulated 75,486 Chrome Web Store install-count bucket totals across all 737 extensions, including 58,318 installs on 516 extensions that were active when the corpus was collected.
  • The extensions mainly targeted Russian-speaking users seeking access to blocked services, and 690 of 734 extensions in the source dataset were Russian-targeted by at least one of Socket’s tests.
  • Socket found that all 200 premium server hostnames tested for Japan, Singapore, Canada, Australia, and Turkey returned no A record, while those entries were marked as premium in the shipped server lists.

DeadLock ransomware uses blockchain to resist infrastructure takedown — Should Read

DeadLock ransomware is using Polygon blockchain smart contracts and decentralized services to keep victim communications and leak-site infrastructure online even if traditional servers are taken down. Microsoft says the setup improves resilience but still depends on components like proxies, RPC endpoints, and Wasabi-hosted files that can be disrupted.

  • DeadLock ransomware uses decentralized infrastructure backed by blockchain services to support victim communications and data-leak activity.
  • Microsoft researchers found that DeadLock stores configuration data and leak-site posts on the Polygon blockchain, with its HTML chat page retrieving the current chat-proxy address through a read-only eth_call.
  • DeadLock also uses the decentralized Session network to encrypt victim communications and provides access to stolen files hosted on the Wasabi cloud service.
  • Microsoft reported that DeadLock avoids countries in the former Soviet Union and Commonwealth of Independent States region, as well as Iran, Syria, Oman, and Yemen.
  • DeadLock encrypts selected non-system directories with per-file XChaCha20 keys protected by Curve25519 and renames encrypted files with a victim-specific identifier and the .dlock extension.

Google says Chrome cuts 7 billion unwanted Android notifications a day to fight abuse — Should Read

Google says Chrome’s layered anti-abuse defenses cut more than 7 billion unwanted Android notifications per day by automatically revoking permissions, limiting abusive sites, and detecting coordinated malicious notification networks. Users can review or restore blocked notification permissions in Chrome settings or Safety Hub.

  • Google says Chrome's anti-abuse systems reduced unwanted notifications on Android by more than 7 billion per day during the first quarter of 2026.
  • Google says notification abuse is increasingly used to distribute scams, malware, phishing attempts, and fraudulent payment requests.
  • Chrome can automatically remove notification permissions from inactive websites and from sites that repeatedly trigger suspicious-notification warnings.
  • Google analyzes behavior across networks of related websites, including coordinated service-worker activity, to identify groups distributing malicious or deceptive notifications.
  • Sites classified as disruptive can be limited to 1,000 messages per minute, with excess requests returning an HTTP 429 error.
